lessons.title: Essential Nutrients for Avocado
lessons.body: Avocado trees need 16 essential nutrients to grow well and produce good fruit. The main ones are nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), sulfur (S), zinc (Zn), boron (B), iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu), molybdenum (Mo), chlorine (Cl), nickel (Ni), and oxygen, hydrogen, and carbon from air and water. In Africa, many soils are old and weathered, so they often lack nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, zinc, and boron. For example, sandy soils in Ghana or Kenya may have less than 0.1% nitrogen, which is very low. Avocado trees need these nutrients for specific jobs. Nitrogen makes leaves green and helps trees grow. Phosphorus helps roots and flowers. Potassium helps fruit size and quality. Zinc prevents small, mottled leaves. Boron helps fruit set and prevents misshapen fruit. Iron keeps leaves green in high-pH soils. Without enough nutrients, trees grow slowly, produce few fruits, and fruits may be small or drop early. You can see signs: yellow leaves mean lack of nitrogen; purple leaves mean lack of phosphorus; small leaves with yellow spots mean lack of zinc. But sometimes signs are not clear. That's why soil and leaf testing is important. As a smallholder, you can start by applying manure or compost, which provides many nutrients. But to get high yields, you may need to add specific fertilizers. Remember, too much of a nutrient can also harm trees. For example, too much nitrogen can cause lots of leaves but few fruits. Too much boron can kill leaves. So always follow recommendations from soil tests or local extension officers. In Africa, organizations like the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) provide guides for avocado nutrition. Start by learning the signs of deficiency and apply nutrients carefully.

lessons.title: Soil and Leaf Tissue Testing
lessons.body: Soil and leaf testing tell you exactly what nutrients your avocado trees need. Without testing, you are guessing. In Africa, many farmers skip testing because they think it is expensive or difficult. But it can save you money and increase yields. Soil testing: Take soil samples from around the tree canopy, about 30 cm deep, from 10-15 spots in your orchard. Mix them in a clean bucket, then take about 500g to a laboratory. In Kenya, you can send samples to KALRO or private labs like Crop Nutrition Laboratory Services (Cropnuts). The test costs about 2,000-5,000 KES (20-50 USD). The report will show soil pH, organic matter, and levels of nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, and boron. It will also give recommendations on how much fertilizer to apply. Leaf testing: This shows what the tree has actually taken up. Take leaf samples from the middle of the current season's growth, from 4-6 month old leaves. Collect 20-30 leaves from different trees, avoid diseased or sunburnt leaves. Send them to a lab. Leaf testing is best done when trees are not flushing new leaves or fruiting heavily. The lab will compare nutrient levels to standard ranges. For avocado, optimal leaf nitrogen is 2.0-2.5%, phosphorus 0.1-0.3%, potassium 1.0-2.0%, zinc 30-100 ppm, boron 20-60 ppm. If levels are below, you need to fertilize. If above, reduce. In Africa, leaf testing is less common but very useful. Some labs like Cropnuts in Kenya offer both soil and leaf testing. If you cannot afford testing, you can use visual symptoms and local recommendations, but testing is more accurate. Always test before planting and then every 1-2 years. This helps you avoid over-fertilizing, which wastes money and can pollute water.

lessons.title: Fertilizer Types and Application Methods
lessons.body: Fertilizers come in many forms: inorganic (mineral) and organic (manure, compost). In Africa, common inorganic fertilizers include urea (46% N), calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN, 27% N), triple superphosphate (TSP, 46% P2O5), muriate of potash (MOP, 60% K2O), and compound fertilizers like NPK 17-17-17. Organic fertilizers include cattle manure (about 0.5% N, 0.2% P, 0.5% K), poultry manure (3% N, 2% P, 1% K), and compost. Application methods: 1) Broadcasting: Spreading fertilizer evenly under the tree canopy, then incorporating into soil. Good for phosphorus and potassium. 2) Banding: Placing fertilizer in a band around the drip line. 3) Fertigation: Injecting soluble fertilizers into irrigation water. Common in South Africa and increasingly in Kenya. 4) Foliar spraying: Spraying diluted fertilizer on leaves, good for quick correction of micronutrient deficiencies like zinc and boron. For young trees (1-3 years), apply 100-200g of NPK 17-17-17 per tree per year, split into 2-3 applications. For mature trees (5+ years), apply 1-2 kg of NPK per tree per year, plus additional nitrogen. Always apply fertilizer when soil is moist, not dry. Avoid placing fertilizer directly against the trunk, as it can burn. For organic manure, apply 10-20 kg per mature tree per year, spread under the canopy. In Africa, many farmers use manure because it is cheap and improves soil. But manure alone may not supply enough nutrients for high yields. Combine organic and inorganic for best results. Always read fertilizer labels and follow recommended rates. Over-application can harm trees and waste money.

lessons.title: Macronutrient Management (N, P, K)
lessons.body: Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) are needed in large amounts. Nitrogen: Avocado trees need nitrogen for leaf growth and fruit production. A mature tree needs about 0.5-1.0 kg of actual N per year. In Kenya, common sources are urea (46% N) or CAN (27% N). Apply in split doses: one-third at flowering, one-third at fruit set, one-third after harvest. Too little N causes yellow leaves and poor growth; too much causes excessive leaf growth and few fruits. Phosphorus: Important for root development and flowering. Avocado trees need about 0.1-0.2 kg P2O5 per year. Apply as TSP or in NPK blends. Phosphorus is less mobile in soil, so place it near roots. In acidic soils (pH below 5.5), phosphorus is less available; apply lime to raise pH to 6.0-6.5. Potassium: Needed for fruit size, quality, and disease resistance. A mature tree needs about 0.5-1.0 kg K2O per year. Apply as MOP or potassium sulfate. Potassium deficiency causes small fruits and leaf scorch. In sandy soils, potassium leaches easily, so split applications. In Africa, many soils are deficient in N and P, but K may be adequate in some volcanic soils. Use soil tests to guide. For example, if soil test shows low N, apply 1 kg urea per tree; if low P, apply 0.5 kg TSP; if low K, apply 0.8 kg MOP. Always adjust based on tree age and yield. Remember, balanced nutrition is key. Too much of one nutrient can affect uptake of others. For instance, high potassium can reduce magnesium uptake. So follow soil test recommendations and apply in splits. In Kenya, KALRO recommends for mature avocado: 1 kg NPK 17-17-17 per tree per year plus 0.5 kg urea, split into three applications.

lessons.title: Micronutrient Management (Zn, B, Fe)
lessons.body: Micronutrients are needed in small amounts but are critical. Zinc (Zn), boron (B), and iron (Fe) are the most common deficiencies in African avocado orchards. Zinc deficiency: Causes small, narrow leaves with yellow spots between veins (mottled). New leaves are affected first. In Kenya, many soils are deficient in zinc. To correct, spray trees with zinc sulfate (0.5% solution, i.e., 50g in 10 liters of water) 2-3 times per year, at flushing and after fruit set. You can also apply zinc sulfate to soil at 20-50g per tree per year. Boron deficiency: Causes misshapen fruits, corky areas inside, and dieback of growing tips. Boron is toxic in excess, so be careful. Apply borax or boric acid at 10-20g per mature tree per year, broadcast under canopy. For quick correction, spray 0.1% borax solution (10g in 10 liters). Do not exceed recommended rates. Iron deficiency: Causes yellow leaves with green veins (interveinal chlorosis), especially on high-pH soils (pH above 7.0). Common in parts of Kenya and Tanzania. To correct, lower soil pH by adding elemental sulfur or organic matter. Spray with chelated iron (Fe-EDDHA) at 0.5g per liter, 2-3 times. In Africa, micronutrient deficiencies are often linked to soil erosion and continuous cropping without replenishment. Regular leaf testing helps detect deficiencies early. For smallholders, a simple approach is to apply well-decomposed manure, which contains micronutrients. But for severe deficiencies, specific sprays are needed. Always follow label instructions and avoid over-application, especially boron, which can kill trees. In South Africa, commercial growers use fertigation with micronutrient mixes. In Kenya, KALRO recommends foliar sprays of zinc and boron for avocado. Remember, healthy trees with good organic matter are less likely to have micronutrient problems.

lessons.title: Organic Fertilization Strategies
lessons.body: Organic fertilization uses natural materials like manure, compost, and cover crops to feed avocado trees. It improves soil health, water holding capacity, and nutrient availability. In Africa, where inorganic fertilizers can be expensive, organic strategies are essential. Manure: Cattle, goat, poultry, and rabbit manure are good sources. Apply 10-20 kg of well-decomposed cattle manure per mature tree per year, spread under the canopy but away from the trunk. Poultry manure is richer; use 5-10 kg per tree. Fresh manure can burn roots, so compost it first. Compost: Make compost from crop residues, kitchen waste, and animal manure. A good compost has about 1-2% nitrogen. Apply 20-30 kg per tree per year. Compost also adds organic matter, which helps sandy soils hold nutrients. Cover crops: Plant legumes like beans, cowpeas, or lablab between trees. They fix nitrogen from the air and add organic matter when cut. In Kenya, farmers use desmodium and mucuna. Mulching: Spread dry grass, leaves, or crop residues around the tree base. Mulch conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and adds nutrients as it decomposes. Green manures: Grow fast-growing plants like tithonia (Mexican sunflower) and incorporate into soil. Tithonia is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. In Africa, many farmers use tithonia as a cheap fertilizer. Liquid fertilizers: Make compost tea or manure tea by soaking manure in water for 1-2 weeks, then dilute and apply to soil or leaves. This gives a quick nutrient boost. Combining organic and inorganic: For best results, combine organic materials with small amounts of inorganic fertilizers. For example, apply manure plus 200g of NPK per tree. This provides both immediate and long-term nutrients. Organic farming also improves soil life, which helps roots access nutrients. In Ethiopia, a study showed that combining compost with NPK increased avocado yields by 30% compared to NPK alone. Start by making compost and using manure from your animals. Over time, you will see healthier trees and better fruits.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most important for making leaves green and promoting growth?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is a key component of chlorophyll, which makes leaves green and drives vegetative growth.

quiz.q: What is the main role of phosphorus in avocado trees?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus is essential for root growth, flower formation, and energy transfer in the plant.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes misshapen fruits and corky areas inside?
quiz.explanation: Boron is critical for fruit set and development; deficiency leads to misshapen fruits and internal corkiness.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for taking soil samples in an avocado orchard?
quiz.explanation: Soil samples are typically taken at 30 cm depth to represent the root zone where most nutrients are taken up.

quiz.q: Which laboratory in Kenya is mentioned for soil and leaf testing?
quiz.explanation: Cropnuts is a private laboratory in Kenya that offers soil and leaf testing services for farmers.

quiz.q: What is the optimal leaf nitrogen range for avocado?
quiz.explanation: For healthy avocado trees, leaf nitrogen should be between 2.0% and 2.5% according to standard guidelines.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is a common source of nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Urea contains 46% nitrogen and is widely used as a nitrogen fertilizer.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: B) Injecting fertilizer into irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the application of fertilizers through irrigation systems, allowing precise nutrient delivery.

quiz.q: For a mature avocado tree, how much actual nitrogen is recommended per year?
quiz.explanation: Mature avocado trees typically require about 0.5 to 1.0 kg of actual nitrogen per year, split into applications.

quiz.q: Which soil pH range is best for avocado nutrient availability?
quiz.explanation: Avocado trees grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soils with pH between 5.5 and 6.5, where nutrients are most available.

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of zinc sulfate as a foliar spray?
quiz.explanation: A 0.5% zinc sulfate solution (50g in 10 liters of water) is commonly used for foliar correction of zinc deficiency.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes yellow leaves with green veins?
quiz.explanation: Iron deficiency leads to interveinal chlorosis, where leaves turn yellow but veins remain green.

quiz.q: What is a good organic source of nitrogen for avocado trees?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure is rich in nitrogen (about 3%) and is an excellent organic fertilizer for avocado.

quiz.q: How much well-decomposed cattle manure should be applied per mature avocado tree per year?
quiz.explanation: Applying 10-20 kg of cattle manure per mature tree per year provides nutrients and improves soil structure.

quiz.q: Which cover crop is mentioned as a nitrogen-fixing legume for avocado orchards?
quiz.explanation: Cowpeas are a legume that fixes atmospheric nitrogen and can be used as a cover crop in avocado orchards.

quiz.q: What is the danger of over-applying boron?
options: B) It can kill leaves and trees
quiz.explanation: Boron is toxic in excess; over-application can cause leaf burn, dieback, and even tree death.

quiz.q: Which method is best for correcting a severe micronutrient deficiency quickly?
quiz.explanation: Foliar spraying delivers nutrients directly to leaves for rapid absorption and quick correction of deficiencies.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of NPK 17-17-17 for a mature avocado tree per year?
quiz.explanation: Mature avocado trees generally require 1-2 kg of NPK 17-17-17 per year, split into multiple applications.

quiz.q: Which organic material is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium and is used as green manure?
quiz.explanation: Tithonia (Mexican sunflower) is a fast-growing plant that accumulates nutrients and can be used as green manure.

quiz.q: What is compost tea?
options: B) Liquid fertilizer made by soaking compost in water
quiz.explanation: Compost tea is made by steeping compost in water, which extracts nutrients and beneficial microbes for liquid fertilization.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is important for fruit size and quality?
quiz.explanation: Potassium plays a key role in fruit development, improving size, color, and sugar content.

quiz.q: What is the first step in soil testing?
quiz.explanation: Collecting representative soil samples is the first step before sending them to a laboratory for analysis.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient is often deficient in high-pH soils?
quiz.explanation: Iron becomes less available in high-pH (alkaline) soils, leading to deficiency in avocado trees.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of borax for soil application per mature avocado tree?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10-20 g of borax per mature tree per year to correct boron deficiency without risking toxicity.

quiz.q: Which practice helps conserve moisture and adds nutrients as it decomposes?
quiz.explanation: Mulching with organic materials conserves soil moisture, suppresses weeds, and releases nutrients upon decomposition.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of combining organic and inorganic fertilizers?
options: B) It provides both immediate and long-term nutrients
quiz.explanation: Combining organic and inorganic fertilizers supplies readily available nutrients plus improves soil health over time.

quiz.q: Which African country is mentioned for a study showing compost plus NPK increased avocado yields?
quiz.explanation: A study in Ethiopia found that combining compost with NPK increased avocado yields by 30% compared to NPK alone.

quiz.q: What is the main function of potassium in avocado?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is crucial for fruit size, quality, and overall plant health, including disease resistance.

quiz.q: How often should leaf testing be done in an avocado orchard?
quiz.explanation: Leaf testing every 1-2 years helps monitor nutrient status and adjust fertilization programs accordingly.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is a common source of potassium?
quiz.explanation: Muriate of potash (MOP) contains about 60% K2O and is a widely used potassium fertilizer.
